chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: \(10^{20}\) photons of wavelength 660 nm are emitted per second from a lamp. What is the power of the lamp? (Planck's constant \(= 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{Js}\))
solution:
Energy of one photon: \(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{660 \times 10^{-9}} = 3 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\).
Power \(= nE = 10^{20} \times 3 \times 10^{-19} = 30\,\text{W}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: A 2 mW laser operates at a wavelength of 500 nm. The number of photons that will be emitted per second is (Given, Planck's constant \(h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{Js}\), speed of light \(c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\))
solution:
\(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{500 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.96 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\).
\(n = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-3}}{3.96 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 5 \times 10^{15}\) photons per second.

**Assertion:** The \(\text{KE}_{\text{max}}\) of emitted photoelectrons changes only with change in frequency of incident radiation.
**Reason:** The \(\text{KE}_{\text{max}}\) of emitted photoelectrons depends on intensity of incident radiation.
options: Both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
Both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
Assertion is true but reason is false
Both assertion and reason are false
solution:
For a given metal \(K_{\text{max}} = h\nu - \phi\) changes only when the frequency changes, so the assertion is true.
\(K_{\text{max}}\) does not depend on intensity; intensity changes only the number of photoelectrons. The reason is false.

stem: \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are maximum KE of photoelectrons emitted when wavelengths \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) respectively are incident on a metallic surface. If \(\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_2\), then relation between \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) is
solution:
\(\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_2\) means photon energy \(E_1 = \frac{E_2}{3}\).
\(K_1 = \frac{E_2}{3} - \phi\) while \(\frac{K_2}{3} = \frac{E_2}{3} - \frac{\phi}{3}\).
Since \(\phi > \frac{\phi}{3}\), \(K_1 < \frac{K_2}{3}\).

stem: A photocell is illuminated by a small bright point source at a distance 1 m away. When the same source of light is placed at 2 m away, the electrons emitted by the photocathode is
options: energy electrons become \(\frac{1}{4}\) of previous energy
number of electrons become \(\frac{1}{4}\) of previous number
number of electron become \(\frac{1}{2}\) of previous number
solution:
For a point source, intensity \(\propto \frac{1}{r^2}\). Doubling the distance makes the intensity, and so the number of photoelectrons, \(\frac{1}{4}\) of before.
The energy and momentum of each electron depend on frequency only and do not change.

stem: Light with energy flux \(36\,\text{W/cm}^2\) is incident on a well polished metal square plate of side 2 cm. The force experienced by it is
solution:
A well polished plate reflects fully, so \(F = \frac{2IA}{c}\).
\(IA = 36\,\text{W/cm}^2 \times 4\,\text{cm}^2 = 144\,\text{W}\).
\(F = \frac{2 \times 144}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 9.6 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{N} = 0.96\,\mu\text{N}\).

stem: \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) are work functions of two different photometals (\(W_2 > W_1\)). The same radiation but with frequency more than threshold frequencies of above two metals falls on two metals separately. If \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) are the photo-currents and \(K_1\), \(K_2\) are maximum KE of ejected electrons from two metals then
solution:
The same radiation delivers the same number of photons per second to each metal, so the photocurrents are equal: \(I_1 = I_2\).
\(K = h\nu - W\); since \(W_1 < W_2\), \(K_1 > K_2\).

**Statement I:** Two bulbs emitting monochromatic lights of blue and red colours have same power, then number of photons emitted per second by red bulb is more than blue colour bulb.
**Statement II:** When light energy in the form of photons incident normally on an absorbing surface, it causes pressure on it.
options: I is correct and II is incorrect
I is incorrect and II is correct
solution:
Statement I: \(n = \frac{P\lambda}{hc}\); red light has the longer wavelength, so at equal power the red bulb emits more photons. True.
Statement II: photons carry momentum \(\frac{h}{\lambda}\), so absorbed photons transfer momentum and exert radiation pressure. True.

solution:
\(\frac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi = E\) and \(\frac{hc}{\lambda'} - \phi = 2E\).
So \(\frac{hc}{\lambda'} = E + \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{E\lambda + hc}{\lambda}\), giving \(\lambda' = \frac{hc\lambda}{E\lambda + hc}\).

stem: A lamp emits monochromatic green light uniformly in all directions. The lamp is 3% efficient in converting electrical power to electromagnetic waves and consumes 100 W of power. The amplitude of the electric field associated with the electromagnetic radiation at a distance of 5m from the lamp will be nearly
solution:
Radiated power \(= 3\% \times 100 = 3\,\text{W}\). Intensity at 5 m: \(I = \frac{3}{4\pi(5)^2} = 9.55 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{W/m}^2\).
\(I = \frac{1}{2}c\varepsilon_0 E_0^2\), so \(E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2I}{c\varepsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 9.55 \times 10^{-3}}{3 \times 10^{8} \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}}} \approx 2.68\,\text{V/m}\).

stem: In an experiment on photoelectric effect, the frequency \(\nu\) of incident light is plotted against the stopping potential \(V_0\). The work function of the photoelectric surface is given by
solution:

So \(\phi = e \times OB\), which in electron volt is numerically equal to OB. OA is the threshold frequency and the slope is \(\frac{h}{e}\).

stem: The minimum light intensity that can be perceived by the eye is about \(10^{-10}\,\text{W/m}^2\). The number of photons of wavelength \(5.6 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\) that must enter the pupil of area \(10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\) per sec for vision is approximately (\(h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J-sec}\))
solution:
Power entering the pupil: \(10^{-10} \times 10^{-6} = 10^{-16}\,\text{W}\).
Photon energy: \(\frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{5.6 \times 10^{-7}} = 3.54 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\).
\(n = \frac{10^{-16}}{3.54 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 283 \approx 3 \times 10^{2}\) photons per second.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
**Statement A:** In the wave picture of light, intensity of light is determined by square of the amplitude of the wave.
**Statement B:** In the photon picture of light, intensity of light is determined by the number of photons crossing an unit area per unit time.
Select the correct option.
options: Both statement A and statement B are false
Both statement A and statement B are true
solution: In the wave picture intensity \(\propto\) (amplitude)\(^2\). In the photon picture intensity is the energy carried by photons crossing unit area per unit time, so for a given frequency it is set by the photon flux. Both statements are true.

stem: The maximum velocity of an electron emitted by light of wavelength \(\lambda\) incident on the surface of a metal of work function \(\phi\), is
solution:
\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi = \frac{hc - \lambda\phi}{\lambda}\).
\(v = \left[\frac{2(hc - \lambda\phi)}{m\lambda}\right]^{1/2}\).

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
In photoelectric emission of an electron when a light incidents on the photo-metal. Match the following:

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A) As intensity of incident light increases with a frequency more than threshold frequency | P) Photocurrent decreases |
| B) As frequency of incident radiation increases with same intensity | Q) \(\text{KE}_{\text{max}}\) becomes equal to zero |
| C) As frequency of incident radiation is equal to threshold frequency | R) Photocurrent increases |
| D) As distance of source of light increased from photometal, keeping frequency same | S) \(\text{KE}_{\text{max}}\) of photoelectrons increases |
options: A - R, B - S, C - Q, D - P
A - R, B - P, C - Q, D - S
A - S, B - R, C - Q, D - P
A - P, B - Q, C - R, D - S
solution:
A: more intensity, more photons, so photocurrent increases (R). B: higher frequency raises \(\text{KE}_{\text{max}}\) (S).
C: at threshold frequency \(\text{KE}_{\text{max}} = h\nu_0 - \phi = 0\) (Q). D: moving the source away lowers intensity, so photocurrent decreases (P).

stem: Einstein's photo electric equation is \(E_k = h\nu - \phi\). In this equation \(E_k\) refers to
options: KE of all the emitted electrons
mean of all the emitted electrons
solution: \(h\nu - \phi\) is the energy left to an electron that loses nothing on the way out, so \(E_k\) is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
From the photoelectric effect experiment, following observations are made. Identify which of these are correct.
A) The stopping potential depends only on the work function of metal.
B) The saturation current increases as the intensity of incident light increases
C) The maximum KE of a photoelectron depends on the intensity of incident light
D) Photo-electric effect can be explained using wave theory of light.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
solution:
A is wrong: stopping potential depends on frequency as well as work function. C is wrong: \(K_{\text{max}}\) does not depend on intensity. D is wrong: wave theory cannot explain the effect.
Only B is correct: saturation current rises with intensity.

\(M_2\) has the larger threshold frequency, so the larger work function; at the same frequency it gives smaller KE. S2 is incorrect.

Photon energy: \(\frac{12400}{2000} = 6.2\,\text{eV}\). \(\phi = 6.2 - 4 = 2.2\,\text{eV}\).

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: In photoelectric experiment the plot between anode potential and photoelectric current is shown in the figure. Which of the following is correct?
options: Frequency of light corresponding to 'A' is same as that of 'B' and is different that corresponding to 'C'
Frequency of light corresponding to 'A' is different from B & intensities are the same
Frequency corresponding to B is same as that of C, but intensities are different
Frequency corresponding to B is different from that of C and intensities are different
solution:
A and B have the same stopping potential, so the same frequency; their saturation currents differ, so their intensities differ.
C has a larger stopping potential, so a different (higher) frequency, with the same saturation current as B. So A and B share a frequency that differs from C's.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: A photon of energy E ejects a photoelectron from a metal surface whose work function is \(W_0\). If this electron enters into a uniform magnetic field of induction B in a direction perpendicular to the field and describes a circular path of radius 'r', then the radius 'r' is given by (in the usual notation)
solution:
\(K = E - W_0\), so \(p = mv = \sqrt{2m(E - W_0)}\).
In the field \(evB = \frac{mv^2}{r}\), so \(r = \frac{mv}{eB} = \frac{\sqrt{2m(E - W_0)}}{eB}\).

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: When a point source of monochromatic light is at a distance of 0.2 m from a photoelectric cell, the cut-off voltage and the saturation current are 0.6 volt and 18 mA respectively. If the same source is placed 0.6 m away from the photoelectric cell, then
options: The stopping potential will be 0.2 V
The stopping potential will be 0.6 V
The saturation current will be 6 mA
The saturation current will be 18 mA
solution:
Stopping potential depends only on frequency, so it stays 0.6 V.
Intensity \(\propto \frac{1}{r^2}\): tripling the distance makes the saturation current \(\frac{18}{9} = 2\,\text{mA}\), so neither 6 mA nor 18 mA is right.

A photon does give its whole energy to one electron, so the reason is correct.

solution:

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
The graph between \(\frac{1}{\lambda}\) and stopping potential (\(V_0\)) of three metals having work functions \(\phi_1\), \(\phi_2\) and \(\phi_3\) in an experiment of photoelectric effect is plotted as shown in the figure. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct? (Here \(\lambda\) is the wavelength of the incident ray)
a) Ratio of work functions \(\phi_1 : \phi_2 : \phi_3 = 1 : 2 : 4\)
b) Ratio of work functions \(\phi_1 : \phi_2 : \phi_3 = 4 : 2 : 1\)
c) \(\tan\theta\) is directly proportional to \(\frac{hc}{e}\)
solution:
\(V_0 = \frac{hc}{e}\cdot\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{\phi}{e}\): the \(\frac{1}{\lambda}\)-axis intercept is \(\frac{\phi}{hc}\), so \(\phi \propto\) intercept.
Intercepts 0.001, 0.002, 0.004 give \(\phi_1 : \phi_2 : \phi_3 = 1 : 2 : 4\): a is correct, b is wrong.
\(\tan\theta = \frac{hc}{e}\), so c is correct. Answer: a, c.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Wave nature of light cannot explain photoelectric effect because in photoelectric effect, it is seen that
options: For the frequency of light below a certain value, the photoelectric effect does not take place, irrespective of intensity
maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons is independent of intensity of radiation
There is no time lag between the incidence of radiation and emission of electrons
solution: Wave theory predicts emission at any frequency for enough intensity, \(K_{\text{max}}\) rising with intensity, and a delay while energy builds up. The threshold frequency, the intensity-independent \(K_{\text{max}}\) and the instant emission all contradict it.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: When a point source of light is at a distance of 50 cm from a photoelectric cell, the cut-off voltage is found to be \(V_0\). If the same source is placed at a distance of 1m from the cell, then the cut-off voltage will be
solution: Moving the source changes only the intensity at the cell. Cut-off voltage depends on frequency and work function, so it stays \(V_0\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: As the intensity of incident light increases
options: Kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons increases
Kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons decreases
solution: Higher intensity means more photons per second, so more photoelectrons and a larger photocurrent. Their kinetic energy does not change.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The work functions for metals A, B and C are respectively 1.92 eV, 2.0 eV and 5 eV. According to Einstein's equation the metals which will emit photoelectrons for a radiation of wavelength \(4100\,\mathring{\text{A}}\) is/are
solution:
\(E = \frac{12400}{4100} \approx 3.0\,\text{eV}\).
This exceeds the work functions of A (1.92 eV) and B (2.0 eV) but not C (5 eV), so only A and B emit.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The figure shows a plot of photocurrent versus anode potential for a photosensitive surface for three different radiations. Which one of the following is a correct statement?
options: Curves b and c represent incident radiations of same frequency having same intensity
Curves a and b represent incident radiations of different frequencies and different intensities
Curves a and b represent incident radiations of same frequency but of different intensities
Curves b and c represent incident radiations of different frequencies and different intensities
solution:
Curves a and b meet the axis at the same retarding potential, so the same frequency; their saturation currents differ, so their intensities differ.
Curve c has a larger stopping potential (higher frequency) but the same saturation current as b, so b and c differ in frequency only.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
**Assertion:** There is almost no time-lag between the incidence of light and the emission of photoelectrons.
**Reason:** A photon transfers almost all its energy to a single electron in a metal.
options: Both assertion and reason are correct and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both assertion and reason are correct but reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion
Assertion is correct, but reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but reason is correct
solution:
**Note:** The book's key gives option (2). The reason is the standard explanation of the assertion, so (1) is used here.

Emission starts within about \(10^{-9}\,\text{s}\) of the light arriving. In the photon picture one photon gives its energy to one electron in a single event, so no time is needed for an electron to build up energy. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.
reasoning: Standard assertion-reason pair; some treatments call the reason true but not the explanation. The one-photon, one-electron transfer is the textbook reason for zero time lag, so option 1 is the most defensible. | Judgement question: the one-photon, one-electron transfer is the textbook explanation of the absence of time lag.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: When ultraviolet light is incident on a photocell, its stopping potential is \(V_0\) and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectric is \(K_{\text{max}}\). When X-rays are incident on the same cell, then (\(V_0\) - stopping potential)
solution: X-rays have a much higher frequency than ultraviolet light, so \(K_{\text{max}} = h\nu - \phi\) increases, and \(V_0 = \frac{K_{\text{max}}}{e}\) increases with it.
reasoning: Same question as 25.1 Q39.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Light of frequency 4.5 times the threshold frequency is incident on photosensitive material. If the frequency is halved and intensity is doubled, then the photocurrent becomes
solution:
**Note:** The book's key gives option (2), which treats the photocurrent as proportional to intensity alone. The current follows the number of photons, which here becomes four times.

Halved, the frequency is \(2.25\nu_0\), still above threshold, so emission continues.
Photons per second \(= \frac{I}{h\nu}\): doubling I and halving \(\nu\) multiplies this by \(2 \times 2 = 4\).
So the photocurrent is quadrupled.
reasoning: Option 1 printed 'quadrapled'; spelling fixed. | If the setter treats photocurrent simply as proportional to intensity, the intended answer would be 'doubled' (option 2). Counting photons (\(I / h\nu\)) gives quadrupled, which is the physically correct reading. | Photocurrent is proportional to photon flux I/(h nu), not to I: x4, option 1.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: de-Broglie wavelength of a proton and an alpha particle accelerated through potential difference \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) respectively are equal, then ratio of \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) is
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\). Equal wavelengths need \(m_p e V_1 = (4m_p)(2e)V_2\).
So \(V_1 = 8V_2\): \(V_1 : V_2 = 8 : 1\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The ratio of de-Broglie wavelengths of proton, deuteron and alpha particle accelerated through 100 V, 50 V and 12.5 V respectively is
solution:
\(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{mqV}}\). Proton: \(m \cdot e \cdot 100\); deuteron: \(2m \cdot e \cdot 50\); alpha: \(4m \cdot 2e \cdot 12.5\).
Each product is \(100\,me\), so the wavelengths are in the ratio \(1 : 1 : 1\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The de-Broglie wavelength of an electron and the wavelength of a photon are the same. The ratio between the energy of that photons and the momentum of that electron is (c - speed of light, h - planck's constant)
solution:
Photon energy \(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\); electron momentum \(p = \frac{h}{\lambda}\).
\(\frac{E}{p} = c\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: If the KE of a particle is increased to 16 times of its previous value, the percentage change in de-Broglie wavelength of the particle is
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\): KE 16 times makes \(\lambda\) one quarter.
Change \(= \frac{\lambda - \lambda/4}{\lambda} \times 100 = 75\%\) (a decrease).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: If the momentum of an electron is changed by P, the de-Broglie wavelength associated with its changes by 0.5%. The initial momentum of electron will be
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{p}\), so \(\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{\Delta p}{p}\).
\(\frac{P}{p} = 0.005\), so \(p = \frac{P}{0.005} = 200P\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
Match the following.

| Particle accelerated through a potential difference in volts 'V' | Associated de-broglie wavelength in angstrom |
|---|---|
| A) Electron | P) \(\lambda = \frac{0.101}{\sqrt{V}}\) |
| B) Proton | Q) \(\lambda = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\) |
| C) Deuteron | R) \(\lambda = \frac{0.286}{\sqrt{V}}\) |
| D) \(\alpha\) - particle | S) \(\lambda = \frac{0.202}{\sqrt{V}}\) |
options: A - Q, B - R, C - S, D - P
A - R, B - Q, C - P, D - S
A - P, B - Q, C - S, D - R
A - S, B - P, C - Q, D - R
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\). Electron: \(\frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\,\mathring{\text{A}}\) (Q). Proton: \(\frac{0.286}{\sqrt{V}}\) (R).
Deuteron (mass \(2m_p\)): \(\frac{0.286}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{V}} = \frac{0.202}{\sqrt{V}}\) (S). Alpha (\(4m_p\), \(2e\)): \(\frac{0.286}{\sqrt{8}\sqrt{V}} = \frac{0.101}{\sqrt{V}}\) (P).
reasoning: Printed 'Deutron'; spelling fixed to Deuteron.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Find the de-Broglie wavelength of the electron with kinetic energy of 10 KeV.
solution:
For an electron \(\lambda = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\,\mathring{\text{A}}\) with \(V = 10^{4}\,\text{V}\) for 10 keV.
\(\lambda = \frac{12.27}{100} \approx 0.123\,\mathring{\text{A}}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The de-Broglie wavelength of a particle having kinetic energy E is \(\lambda\). How much extra energy must be given to this particle so that the de-Broglie wavelength reduces to 25% of initial value
solution:
\(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{E}}\). For \(\lambda\) to become \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\), the energy must become \(16E\).
Extra energy \(= 16E - E = 15E\).
reasoning: Option 1 prints as '16 sqrt2' with no E visible (pencil working nearby); transcribed as printed.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with a temperature 2T and mass 'm' is
solution:
At temperature \(2T\) the mean kinetic energy is \(K = \frac{3}{2}k(2T) = 3kT\).
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{6mkT}}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An electron of mass 'm' when accelerated through a potential difference 'V' has de-Broglie wavelength '\(\lambda\)'. The de-Broglie wavelength associated with a proton of mass 'M' accelerated through the same potential difference will be
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\); same charge magnitude and same V, so \(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\).
\(\lambda_p = \lambda\sqrt{\frac{m}{M}}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An electron of mass 'm' and charge 'e' initially at rest gets accelerated by a constant electric field 'E'. The rate of change of de-Broglie wavelength of this electron at time 't' ignoring relativistic effect is
solution:
Starting from rest, \(p = eEt\), so \(\lambda = \frac{h}{eEt}\).
\(\frac{d\lambda}{dt} = -\frac{h}{eEt^2}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with heavy water at a temperature T(Kelvin) and mass 'm', is
solution:
Thermal kinetic energy \(K = \frac{3}{2}kT\).
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3mkT}}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: If \(\alpha\) - particle, proton and electron move with the same momentum, their respective de-Broglie wavelengths \(\lambda_\alpha\), \(\lambda_p\), \(\lambda_e\) are related as
solution: \(\lambda = \frac{h}{p}\) depends only on momentum. Equal momenta give \(\lambda_\alpha = \lambda_p = \lambda_e\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The de-Broglie wavelength of a photon is twice the de-broglie wavelength of an electron. The velocity of electron is \(v_e = \frac{c}{100}\)
solution:
Photon: \(E_p = \frac{hc}{\lambda_p} = \frac{hc}{2\lambda_e}\). Electron: \(mv = \frac{h}{\lambda_e}\), so \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{hv}{2\lambda_e}\).
\(\frac{E_e}{E_p} = \frac{v}{c} = \frac{1}{100} = 10^{-2}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
**Assertion:** Macroscopic objects in our daily life show wave like properties prominent.
**Reason:** Wavelength of macroscopic objects is very small.
options: Both assertion and reason are correct and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both assertion and reason are correct but reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion
Assertion is correct, but reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but reason is correct
solution: Macroscopic objects have huge momentum, so \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\) is far too small to detect: their wave nature is not seen. The assertion is incorrect; the reason is correct.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The masses of two particles having same kinetic energies are in the ratio 2 : 1. Then their de-broglie wavelengths are in the ratio.
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\); equal K gives \(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\).
\(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}\), so \(1 : \sqrt{2}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Electrons are accelerated through a potential difference V and proton are accelerated through a potential difference 4V. The ratio of de-Broglie wavelength \(\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p}\) is given by (given, \(m_e\) is mass of electron and \(m_p\) is the mass of proton)
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\), with equal charge magnitude.
\(\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\frac{m_p \cdot 4V}{m_e \cdot V}} = 2\sqrt{\frac{m_p}{m_e}}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: A particle P of mass 'm' and initial velocity 'v' collides with a particle Q of mass 'm' at rest. The collision is head on and perfectly inelastic. The ratio of de-Broglie wavelengths associated with particle P before collision and combined mass of P and Q after collision respectively is
solution:
Momentum is conserved in the collision, so P before and the combined mass after have the same momentum \(mv\).
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{p}\) is the same: \(1 : 1\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: If two particles are moving such that their de-Broglie wavelength is same, then correct option among the following is
options: both particles may have same linear momentum
both particles may have different linear momentum
both particles must have same linear momentum
solution:
Equal \(\lambda = \frac{h}{p}\) means equal magnitude of momentum only.
Momentum is a vector, so if they move in the same direction the momenta are the same, and in different directions they differ. Both (1) and (2) are possible.
reasoning: Turns on vector versus magnitude. If the setter meant magnitude only, the intended answer could be option 3 ('must have same linear momentum'). As a vector statement, option 4 is correct.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Choose the correct relation between de-Broglie wavelength of an electron in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) Bohr orbit and radius of the orbit 'r'.
solution:
Bohr's condition \(mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}\) with \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\) gives \(2\pi r = n\lambda\).
So \(\lambda = \frac{2\pi r}{n}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The de-Broglie wavelength of an electron is same as that of a photon. If velocity of electron is 25% of the velocity of light, then the ratio of KE of electron and KE of photon will be
solution:
Equal wavelengths mean equal momenta p.
Electron: \(K_e = \frac{p^2}{2m} = \frac{pv}{2}\). Photon: \(E = pc\).
\(\frac{K_e}{E} = \frac{v}{2c} = \frac{0.25}{2} = \frac{1}{8}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: A nucleus A, with a finite de-Broglie wavelength \(\lambda_A\), undergoes spontaneous fission into two nuclei B and C of equal mass B flies in the same direction as that of A, while C flies in the opposite direction with a velocity equal to half of that of B. The de-Broglie wavelength \(\lambda_B\) and \(\lambda_C\) are respectively
solution:
Let A (mass M) move with V; B and C each have mass \(\frac{M}{2}\), with B at v and C at \(-\frac{v}{2}\).
Momentum: \(MV = \frac{M}{2}v - \frac{M}{2}\cdot\frac{v}{2} = \frac{Mv}{4}\), so \(v = 4V\).
\(p_B = \frac{M}{2}(4V) = 2MV\), \(p_C = \frac{M}{2}(2V) = MV\).
So \(\lambda_B = \frac{\lambda_A}{2}\) and \(\lambda_C = \lambda_A\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: According to de-Broglie hypothesis, de-Broglie wavelength for electron in an orbit of (radius \(4.9 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\)) hydrogen atom is \(10^{-10}\,\text{m}\). The principal quantum number for this electron is (nearer to)
solution:
\(2\pi r = n\lambda\), so \(n = \frac{2\pi r}{\lambda} = \frac{2\pi \times 4.9 \times 10^{-11}}{10^{-10}} \approx 3.08\).
Nearest integer: \(n = 3\).
reasoning: Printed 'principle'; spelling fixed to principal.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An electron is projected with velocity 10 m/s at an angle \(60^\circ\) with horizontal, the de-Broglie wavelength of electron at maximum height of its trajectory (in meter) is (h = planck's constant, M = mass of electron, take h and M in SI unit)
solution:
At the highest point only the horizontal velocity remains: \(10\cos 60^\circ = 5\,\text{m/s}\).
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{Mv} = \frac{h}{5M}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An \(\alpha\)- particle and a proton are fired through the same magnetic field which is perpendicular to their velocity vectors. The \(\alpha\)-particle and the proton move such that radius of curvature of their paths is same. Find the ratio of their de-Broglie wavelengths.
solution:
\(r = \frac{p}{qB}\), so for equal r in the same field \(p \propto q\): \(p_\alpha = 2p_p\).
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{p}\), so \(\lambda_\alpha : \lambda_p = 1 : 2\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Two electrons are moving with the same speed v. One electron enters a region of uniform electric field while the other enters a region of uniform magnetic field, then after sometime, if the de-Broglie wavelengths of the two are \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\), then
solution:
A magnetic force does no work, so the second electron keeps speed v and \(\lambda_2\) is unchanged.
An electric field changes the speed: it can speed the electron up (\(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\)) or slow it down (\(\lambda_1 > \lambda_2\)), depending on the field's direction.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Two bodies of A and B having equal masses are moving in opposite direction with velocity 5 m/s and 10 m/s respectively and colliding elastically. Find the ratio of de-Broglie wavelengths of A and B after collision.
solution:
In a head-on elastic collision of equal masses the velocities are exchanged: A moves off at 10 m/s and B at 5 m/s.
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\), so \(\lambda_A : \lambda_B = \frac{1}{10} : \frac{1}{5} = 1 : 2\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the graph between the kinetic energy of photoelectrons ejected and the frequency of incident radiation is
options: Diagram 1: straight line falling from a positive intercept on the KE axis down to the frequency axis (negative slope)
Diagram 2: straight line of positive slope starting above the frequency axis, touching neither axis
Diagram 3: straight line of positive slope through the origin
Diagram 4: straight line of positive slope starting from a positive intercept on the frequency axis
solution:
\(K_{\text{max}} = h\nu - h\nu_0\): a straight line of slope \(h\), zero at the threshold frequency and absent below it.
So the line starts from a positive intercept on the frequency axis: diagram 4.
reasoning: Same question as 25.1 Q18.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The graph shown below shows variation of de-Broglie wavelength (\(\lambda\)) versus \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\) (where V is accelerating potential for three charged particles of equal charges but different masses.
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mq}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\): the slope is \(\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mq}}\), larger for a smaller mass.
Slopes are in the order B > C > A, so the masses are \(m_A > m_C > m_B\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An electron of mass M and a photon have same energy E. The ratio of de-Broglie wavelength associated with them is
solution:
Electron: \(\lambda_e = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}\). Photon: \(\lambda_{ph} = \frac{hc}{E}\).
\(\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_{ph}} = \frac{E}{c\sqrt{2mE}} = \frac{1}{c}\left(\frac{E}{2m}\right)^{1/2}\).
reasoning: Right edge cut: 'h[ave]', 'de-Bro[glie]' completed. Stem says mass M, options use m (as printed).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: If \(\lambda_0\) is the de-Broglie wavelength for a proton accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. The de-Broglie wavelength for \(\alpha\) particle accelerated through same potential difference
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}\). The alpha particle has \(4\) times the mass and \(2\) times the charge.
\(\lambda_\alpha = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{4 \times 2}} = \frac{\lambda_0}{2\sqrt{2}}\).
reasoning: Right edge cut: 'pro[ton]', 'of' and the second particle after 'for' are cut; read as alpha from a partial glyph. | The second particle was read as an alpha particle from a partial glyph at the cut edge. With that reading the answer is option 3.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: A particle is projected horizontally from top of a tower with a velocity of 10 m/s. The ratio of de-Broglie wavelength of particle when velocity vector makes an angle \(45^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\) with horizontal is
solution:
The horizontal velocity stays 10 m/s, so the speed when the velocity makes angle \(\theta\) is \(\frac{10}{\cos\theta}\).
At \(45^\circ\): \(10\sqrt{2}\,\text{m/s}\); at \(60^\circ\): \(20\,\text{m/s}\).
\(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{v}\): \(\lambda_{45} : \lambda_{60} = 20 : 10\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2} : 1\).
reasoning: Right edge cut: 'of', 'whe[n]' and the second angle '6[0 deg]' completed.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Light described at a place by the equation \(E = 100\,\text{V/m}\,[\sin(5 \times 10^{10}\,\text{s}^{-1})t + \sin(8 \times 10^{15}\,\text{s}^{-1})t]\) falls on a metal surface having work function 2eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is
solution:
The higher angular frequency \(\omega = 8 \times 10^{15}\,\text{s}^{-1}\) gives the most energetic photons: \(\nu = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = 1.27 \times 10^{15}\,\text{Hz}\).
\(E = h\nu = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 1.27 \times 10^{15}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 5.27\,\text{eV}\).
\(K_{\text{max}} = 5.27 - 2 = 3.27\,\text{eV}\).
reasoning: Right edge cut at the closing ')t]'; 'v/m' printed lowercase.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An electron (mass 'm') with an initial velocity \(\vec{v} = v_0\hat{i}\) (\(v_0 > 0\)) is in an electric field \(\vec{E} = -E_0\hat{i}\) (\(E_0\) = constant \(> 0\)). Its de-Broglie wavelength at time 't' is given by
solution:
Force on the electron: \(\vec{F} = -e\vec{E} = eE_0\hat{i}\), along its motion, so \(v = v_0 + \frac{eE_0}{m}t\).
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{mv_0\left(1 + \frac{eE_0 t}{mv_0}\right)} = \frac{\lambda_0}{1 + \frac{eE_0}{mv_0}t}\).
reasoning: Right edge cut: the field's unit vector after '-E0' is not visible; i-hat inferred. Vector arrows not printed (added for v and E). | The unit vector of the field is cut off and was inferred as \(\hat{i}\). With \(-E_0\hat{i}\) the electron speeds up, giving option 1.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: The graph between \(\log E\) and \(\log\lambda\), where E and \(\lambda\) are kinetic energy and de-Broglie wavelength of a proton, then which of the following.
options: Diagram 1: \(\log\lambda\) against \(\log E\), straight line of positive slope through the origin
Diagram 2: straight line of positive slope starting from a positive intercept on the \(\log E\) axis
Diagram 3: straight line of negative slope from the \(\log\lambda\) axis down to the \(\log E\) axis
Diagram 4: straight line of positive slope starting from a positive intercept on the \(\log\lambda\) axis
solution:
\(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}\), so \(\log\lambda = \log\frac{h}{\sqrt{2m}} - \frac{1}{2}\log E\).
This is a straight line of negative slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\) with a positive intercept on the \(\log\lambda\) axis: diagram 3.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
The potential energy of a particle of mass 'm' is given by \(U(x) = \begin{cases} E_0; & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & x > 1 \end{cases}\)
\(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are the de-Broglie wavelengths of the particle, when \(0 \le x \le 1\) and \(x > 1\) respectively. If the total energy of particle is \(2E_0\), then \(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\) will be
solution:
For \(0 \le x \le 1\): \(K_1 = 2E_0 - E_0 = E_0\). For \(x > 1\): \(K_2 = 2E_0\).
\(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\), so \(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{\frac{2E_0}{E_0}} = \sqrt{2}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: A particle which has zero rest mass and non-zero energy and non-zero momentum is
options: electron, moves with speed less than speed of light in vacuum
proton, moves with speed less than speed of light in vacuum
photon, moves with speed equals to speed of light in vacuum
any macroscopic particle, moves with speed equals to speed of light in vacuum
solution: A photon has zero rest mass but energy \(h\nu\) and momentum \(\frac{h}{\lambda}\), and it always travels at c in vacuum. Any particle with rest mass moves slower than c.

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Light of wavelength 400 nm is incident on a metal with work function 2.1 eV. The de-Broglie wavelength of the emitted electron is
solution:
Photon energy \(= \frac{1240}{400} = 3.1\,\text{eV}\), so \(K_{\text{max}} = 3.1 - 2.1 = 1.0\,\text{eV}\).
Smallest wavelength (fastest electron): \(\lambda = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{1}}\,\mathring{\text{A}} = 1.227 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}\).
Slower electrons have longer wavelengths, so \(\lambda \ge 1.227 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}\).

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Choose the only correct statement out of the following
options: Only a charged particle in motion is accompanied by matter waves
Only subatomic particles in motion are accompanied by matter waves
Any particle in motion, whether charged or uncharged, is accompanied by matter waves
No particle, whether at rest or in motion, is ever accompanied by matter waves
solution: \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\) applies to every moving particle, charged or not. It is only noticeable when the momentum is very small.

stem: Electrons used in an electron microscope are accelerated by a voltage of 25 kV. If the voltage is increased to 100 kV then the de-broglie wavelength associated with the electrons would
solution: \(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\). Raising V from 25 kV to 100 kV (4 times) makes \(\lambda\) half, so it decreases by 2 times.
